Introduction to fasteukaryotyping

Angel Luís Robles Fernández

Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and Center for Ecological Research, University of Kansas
Source: vignettes/introduction.Rmd
introduction.Rmd

What is MLST and why distance matrices?

Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST) characterises microbial isolates by the alleles present at a set of housekeeping loci. Given a collection of samples (isolates), each with potentially multiple alleles per locus (due to heterozygosity, mixed infections, or polyploidy), the central question is: how genetically similar are any two samples?

fasteukaryotyping implements the three-method ensemble described by Barratt et al. (2019) (doi:10.1017/S0031182019000581) for computing pairwise genetic distances from MLST haplotype data sheets (HDS).

library(fasteukaryotyping)

The three distance methods

Heuristic distance (euk_heuristic_distance)

Barratt’s unsupervised heuristic mixture-model distance computes, for each locus, a delta value that depends on the number of shared alleles, the allele-set sizes, a per-locus entropy term \(H_{\nu}\), and a frequency-informed penalty \(P\). The per-locus deltas are summed across loci to produce the pairwise distance. Missing loci are imputed with a two-pass mean procedure that matches the original Barratt script.

set.seed(42)
n <- 10
geno <- list(
  matrix(sample(c(1L, 2L, 3L, NA), n * 2, replace = TRUE), nrow = n, ncol = 2),
  matrix(sample(c(1L, 2L, NA), n * 2, replace = TRUE), nrow = n, ncol = 2)
)
d_h <- euk_heuristic_distance(geno, ploidy = c(2L, 2L))
dim(d_h)
## [1] 10 10

Bayesian distance (euk_bayesian_distance)

Plucinski’s naive Bayes genetic distance evaluates, for each pair and locus, three log-likelihoods:

  • ll0: samples are unrelated – every allele drawn independently from the locus allele frequencies.
  • ll1: samples share exactly one allele – the shared allele is the most likely one; remaining alleles drawn independently.
  • ll2 (diploid loci only): samples share both alleles – evaluated over all 2-subsets; missing allele draws get probability \(\epsilon \cdot \min(p_1, p_2)\).

The per-locus values are summed, normalised to a posterior over the three hypotheses, and the distance is the posterior expectation in \([0, 2]\).

d_b <- euk_bayesian_distance(geno, ploidy = c(2L, 2L))
dim(d_b)
## [1] 10 10

Ensemble distance (euk_ensemble_distance)

The ensemble converts each matrix to fractional ranks over the unordered pairs and takes the mean of the two ranks. This copula-style average is invariant to monotone transformations of either distance, producing a consensus value in \([0, 1]\).

d_e <- euk_ensemble_distance(geno, ploidy = c(2L, 2L))
dim(d_e)
## [1] 10 10

Input data format

The core input geno is a list of \(L\) integer matrices (one per locus), each with \(n\) rows (samples) and up to maxMOI columns. Missing alleles are coded as NA (or 0). The ploidy vector specifies whether each locus is haploid (1) or diploid (2).

MLST data is often stored as a Haplotype Data Sheet (HDS): a CSV with a Seq_ID column and one column per haplotype per locus, where presence is marked by "X". Use euk_import_hds() to convert this format into the internal geno list:

hds <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "example_hds.csv",
                             package = "fasteukaryotyping"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
out <- euk_import_hds(hds, locinames = "Hap", ploidy = 2L)
attr(out, "geno")
## [[1]]
##       1_Hap_Hap 2_Hap_Hap
##  [1,]         1         1
##  [2,]         2         2
##  [3,]         1         1
##  [4,]         2         2
##  [5,]         1         1
##  [6,]         1         1
##  [7,]         2         2
##  [8,]         2         2
##  [9,]         1         1
## [10,]         2         2
## [11,]         1         1
## [12,]         2         2

Performance

The C++ implementation uses RcppParallel for multi-threaded pairwise computation. For a dataset of \(n\) samples and \(L\) loci, the heuristic distance processes \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs in parallel per locus, while the Bayesian distance parallelises over the full \(n \times n\) matrix.

Compare the R reference and C++ implementations on the built-in example:

eg <- example_eukaryotyping
system.time({
  d_r <- euk_heuristic_distance(eg$geno, eg$ploidy, use_r = TRUE)
})
##    user  system elapsed 
##   0.011   0.001   0.010
system.time({
  d_cpp <- euk_heuristic_distance(eg$geno, eg$ploidy, use_r = FALSE)
})
##    user  system elapsed 
##   0.001   0.000   0.000
